title: Framework Launches New Couch Keyboard: Pre‑Order the Innovative Portable Keyboard Today
body:
A sleek, wireless touchpad keyboard that doubles as a portable laptop stand is now open for preorder, with a launch price of $99. The new accessory, marketed as the Wireless Touchpad Keyboard, repurposes the same modular hardware found in Framework’s line‑up of repair‑friendly laptops, delivering a thin, low‑profile input surface that folds into a sturdy, ergonomic couch‑friendly platform. Early adopters can secure the device through Framework’s online store, with shipments slated for early next year.

The design merges two functions that have traditionally required separate peripherals: a full‑size keyboard and a touchpad, and a lap‑or‑couch stand that elevates a laptop to a more comfortable viewing angle. By leveraging the same 40 mm thin, aluminum chassis used in Framework’s laptop upgrades, the keyboard maintains a minimal footprint while still offering a tactile typing experience comparable to the brand’s notebook keyboards. Its Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) connection promises low latency and a battery life that the company claims will exceed six months on a single charge, a claim that will be put to the test once the product reaches consumers.

Framework’s entry into the peripheral market comes at a time when the industry is seeing renewed interest in all‑in‑one input devices that can replace the aging “couch keyboard” segment once dominated by Logitech’s K400 series. The K400, introduced in 2013, combined a full‑size keyboard with a built‑in trackpad and quickly became a staple for living‑room computing. However, its plastic build and dated Bluetooth implementation have left room for a modern, more durable alternative. By offering a metal‑body, modular construction, and a price point just shy of $100, Framework positions its new keyboard as a premium upgrade for both remote workers and casual users who prefer a tidy, cable‑free setup.

Beyond the hardware, the product underscores Framework’s broader philosophy of repairability and sustainability. The company has built a reputation on laptops that can be disassembled and upgraded with standard tools, and the Wireless Touchpad Keyboard follows suit. Its internal components—such as the BLE module, battery pack, and key switches—are soldered onto a single board that can be swapped out without specialized equipment. Framework also promises to make spare parts and firmware updates available for at least five years, a commitment that could extend the device’s lifespan far beyond the typical three‑year consumer electronics cycle.

Analysts see the move as a strategic diversification for Framework, which has so far relied heavily on its laptop sales to fund its open‑hardware mission. By expanding into accessories, the company can tap into a larger market segment and generate recurring revenue streams while reinforcing its brand identity. The $99 price tag is competitive when measured against comparable offerings from established peripheral manufacturers, many of which charge $120‑$150 for similar functionality but lack the same emphasis on modularity and long‑term support.

Looking ahead, the success of the Wireless Touchpad Keyboard could influence how other manufacturers approach peripheral design, especially as remote work and hybrid office setups continue to normalize. If Framework’s blend of durability, repair‑friendliness, and affordable pricing resonates with consumers, it may prompt a shift away from disposable, low‑cost accessories toward products built to last. For now, the preorder window offers early adopters a chance to be part of that potential transition, while the broader tech community watches to see whether this modestly priced keyboard can truly dethrone the long‑standing K400 in the living‑room computing arena.
